text.p: The following are the main stories from Wednesday morning's Austrian newspapers:

- Austria's largest bank Bank Austria may bid for the government's stake in Creditanstalt. CA's chairman of the supervisory board Walter Fremuth has confirmed the rumours. Finance Minister Viktor Klima will present the names of all the bidding parties on Monday, December 16.
- The Social Affairs Ministry's draft law on more flexible work hours has been rejected by the conservative junior coalition party and will have to be renegotiated.

- Conservative Vice-Chancellor Wolfgang Schuessel said in the light of mounting criticism of the government he had no plans to press for an early election. However, he said the 1998 and 1999 budgets would be an important test.
- Industrial group Voest-Alpine Industrieanlagenbau expects orders to rise over 20 billion schillings in the near future. Meanwhile talks are being held in the United States on further acquisitions.
- Bank Austria is rumoured to be about to put in a bid for 16 billion schillings to take over Creditanstalt with the help of German bank WestLB.

- Social Democrats have given the go ahead to plans by Defence Minister Werner Fasslabend to buy Dutch Leopard II tanks. Including other acquisitions for Austria's army the Defence Ministry will spend more than seven billion schillings.
- A study by the Chamber of Labour shows the paper industry was lagging behind this year after a profitable performance a year ago.
- Conservative People's Party strongly opposes rumoured plans by Bank Austria to take over Creditanstalt, saying it would cost thousands of jobs.
- Lenzing might cut 400 to 500 jobs if it follows rationalisation plans put forward by consulting firm Arthur D. Little.
- As U.S. carmaker Chrysler plans to expand business in Europe the firm's production plant in Graz, southern Austria, remains the only one in Europe at present.
- Due to the government's austerity programmes and EU membership direct and indirect subsidies have declined by eight billion schillings.
